extracted.intended_audience: federal agency officials, policymakers, administrative law practitioners, ACUS members, and the public interested in administrative procedure
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how the Administrative Conference of the United States develops, adopts, publishes, and follows up on recommendations and related Statements to improve administrative procedure. Covers required metadata and the organizational process for producing recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of ACUS recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: One of ACUS's primary statutory functions is to make recommendations for action by federal agencies, the President, Congress, and the Judicial Conference of the United States to improve administrative procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations should be aimed at improving administrative procedure and can be directed to agencies, the President, Congress, or the Judicial Conference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development by committees with expert support
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations are developed by committees of ACUS members, typically with the support of expert consultants and ACUS staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The development process relies on committee work plus subject-matter consultants and ACUS staff assistance; committees are the primary drafting bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption by full membership at plenary sessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations are adopted by the full membership at twice-yearly plenary sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal adoption requires membership approval at one of the two plenary sessions each year; this is the official mechanism that converts a committee product into an ACUS recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of adopted recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopted recommendations are published on the ACUS website and in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once adopted, recommendations are made publicly available through ACUS's website and are published in the Federal Register to ensure public dissemination and official record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chairman and staff follow-up to encourage implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chairman and ACUS staff undertake activities to encourage federal agencies to carry out recommendations adopted by ACUS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACUS does active follow-up and outreach after adoption to promote agency consideration and implementation of recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statements as distinct but similarly developed products
rubrics_metrics.description: ACUS sometimes adopts “Statements,” which express the agency's views on a particular matter without making a formal recommendation. Statements are developed through the same process as recommendations but typically set forth issues, conclusions from a study, or comments, rather than recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements follow the same committee/consultant/staff/adoption process but differ in content (issues, conclusions, comments) and are not formal recommendations; ACUS has adopted 20 statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended metadata for each recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each listed recommendation entry on the page includes Project, Recommendation number, Adopted on (date), Committee, and an Executive Summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations should provide clear metadata: the project name, a unique recommendation number, adoption date, the responsible committee, and an executive summary to summarize the recommendation's purpose and key points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Summary requirement/content
rubrics_metrics.description: An Executive Summary accompanies each recommendation and summarizes the problem, purpose, and key aspects of the recommendation (e.g., why access to records is needed; what temporary rules are; why adjudication office organization matters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive Summaries should concisely explain the issue the recommendation addresses and the recommended course(s) of action or principles, enabling readers to understand the recommendation’s rationale without reading the full text.
